kurals.tamil:
கருமம் செயஒருவன் கைதூவேன் என்னும்
பெருமையின் பீடுடையது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karumam seya oruvan kaithooven ennum
perumaiyin peedudaiyadhu il.
kurals.meaning: No greatness carries more dignity than a person's resolve, ‘I will not rest my hands from the work of raising my family.’
kurals.elementary: Imagine a girl who promises, ‘I will keep helping my family every day, and I won’t give up when it gets boring.’ Valluvar says that promise, kept day after day, is the proudest thing a person can wear, prouder than any medal.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by naming its ideal: the person who says kai thooven (கைதூவேன், ‘I will not let my hand rest’) in karumam (கருமம், ‘the work’), understood by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as the duty of raising one's kudi (குடி, ‘family, lineage, community’). Peedu (பீடு) means dignity or eminence, so the couplet ranks this self-imposed vow above every other form of perumai (பெருமை, ‘greatness’), the subject of chapter 98. Solomon Pappaiah widens kudi to ‘house and country’, a reading he keeps through the whole chapter, while Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, keeps it to one's own family line. Pope renders it ‘Who says “I’ll do my work, nor slack my hand”, / His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.’ The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For if I ever failed to engage in carefully performing prescribed duties, O Pārtha, certainly all men would follow My path.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that although He needs nothing, He never stops working, because others take their cue from Him.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's ‘I will not rest my hand’, the greatest one refuses to slacken in his work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.23 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; strong match on the vow never to stop working, though the Gita's context is cosmic order rather than family.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher urges full-strength effort in whatever work lies at hand, since the chance to act does not last.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts honour the hand that does not hold back from its task.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a good fit on untiring effort, without the Kural's focus on the family.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands. The Prophet (ﷺ) of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises food earned by one's own labour and holds up the prophet-king David as one who lived by his hands.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats tireless work with one's own hands as a mark of honour.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it praises self-supporting labour, but does not speak directly of raising a family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that no one person completes the great work, but no one may walk away from it either.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's vow ‘I will not slack my hand’ is the same refusal to neglect the work.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:16 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close fit on persistence, though Tarfon speaks of Torah study rather than family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that renown keeps growing for the person who is energetic and disciplined.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say the highest honour belongs to the person of unflagging effort.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 24 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on energy bringing glory, though it adds moral qualities and does not mention family.

jainism.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira urges his disciple Gautama not to slacken now that most of the journey is done, but to press on to the end.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain refrain shares the Kural's refusal to stop before the work is finished, though its goal is liberation, not a family's rise.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the call never to slacken matches, but Jain scripture directs that effort toward renunciation rather than household duty, so this is a next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that honest toil is honourable and only idleness brings shame.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets place honour in the person who keeps working.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 293-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match, and Hesiod's advice is aimed at a household farmer, much like the Kural's.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself, when he is reluctant to leave his bed at dawn, that he is rising to do the work of a human being and was not made merely to lie warm under the blankets.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic emperor treats unflagging effort at one's proper work as the very purpose of a human life.
philosophy.tie_back: His self-command matches the Kural's ‘I will not rest my hand.’
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the wording was not checked against a live translation this session, though the passage is well known.

kurals.tamil:
ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் எனஇரண்டின்
நீள்வினையால் நீளும் குடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Aalvinaiyum aandra arivum ena irandin
neelvinaiyaal neelum kudi.
kurals.meaning: A family grows and lasts through sustained work that combines two things: manly effort and full knowledge.
kurals.elementary: Building a strong treehouse needs two things: strong arms to hammer and a smart plan so it doesn't fall. Valluvar says a family is the same: hard work plus good thinking, kept up for a long time, makes it grow tall.
kurals.university: The couplet names two instruments, aalvinai (ஆள்வினை, ‘manly exertion’, the theme of chapter 62) and aandra arivu (ஆன்ற அறிவு, ‘full, ripened knowledge’), and says that the neelvinai (நீள்வினை, ‘long, unbroken effort’) carried out with both makes the kudi neelum (நீளும், ‘lengthen, extend, flourish’). The play between neel- ‘long’ in the work and neel- ‘lengthen’ in the family is deliberate: duration in effort produces duration in the line. Pope captures this with ‘In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race’s line.’ Kesikan and Varadarasanar both read the two as effort and knowledge joined in uninterrupted action; Karunanidhi adds ‘deep knowledge and perseverance.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore strive for yoga, which is the art of all work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga, the joining of right understanding to action, is the true skill in all work.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's pairing of effort with knowledge, the Gita asks for work guided by understanding.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the Sanskrit yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam (skill in action) fits well, but Prabhupada's devotional rendering moves it away from household effort.

christianity.quote_or_event: The book of Proverbs says that a house is built through wisdom and established by understanding, and that by knowledge its rooms are filled with precious and pleasant riches.
christianity.explanation: The sage teaches that a household rises and endures when skill and understanding work together.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's claim that effort joined to knowledge makes a family grow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; a strong thematic match on wisdom building a house.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Messenger of Allah! Shall I tie it and rely(upon Allah), or leave it loose and rely(upon Allah)?” He said: “Tie it and rely(upon Allah).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells a man to take sensible practical steps and trust God as well, not to trust while doing nothing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's pairing of effort with prudent knowledge matches this joining of practical care to action.
islam.source: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 2517 (sunnah.com; graded Hasan by Darussalam)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it teaches practical prudence with action, but says nothing about a family's growth, and Tirmidhi himself calls this chain gharib.

judaism.quote_or_event: “excellent is the study of the Torah when combined with a worldly occupation, for toil in them both keeps sin out of one’s mind”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel praises a life that joins learning with practical work, warning that learning without labour comes to nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says lasting good comes from two things worked at together: knowledge and labour.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:2 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match on joining knowledge and work, though its stated aim is avoiding sin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “by whatsoever activity a householder earns his living ... at that he becomes skillful and is not lazy. He is endowed with the power of discernment as to the proper ways and means; he is able to carry out and allocate (duties). This is called the accomplishment of persistent effort.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells lay householders that their welfare rests first on diligent, skilful work guided by discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural's formula: effort plus knowledge, kept up, makes a household thrive.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 8.54, Dighajanu (Vyagghapajja) Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks an omitted list of trades); a near one-to-one match addressed to householders.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra opens by teaching that right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together make up the path to liberation; none of them is enough alone.
jainism.explanation: Jainism's three jewels insist that knowledge and conduct must be joined for any real progress.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's two-part recipe of knowledge plus effort echoes this Jain insistence on joining knowing and doing, though the goal is liberation, not a family's rise.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1 (Umasvati, tr. Nathmal Tatia, ‘That Which Is’)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known sutra, not checked verbatim this session; the structural parallel is real but the aims differ, so it is a next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, given tools by Calypso, fells trees and builds his own raft with a craftsman's skill, then steers it home by the stars.
greek_mythology.explanation: His escape needs both hard labour and expert knowledge, working together over days.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hero's way home to his family is opened by effort and knowledge combined.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a fair illustration of skill plus toil, though not a teaching about families.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that virtue sets the right goal while practical wisdom (phronesis) finds the right means, and that a person needs both to act well.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, good character without practical intelligence, or cleverness without good aims, both fall short.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing of effort and knowledge as joint causes of success.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a reasonable structural parallel, though Aristotle pairs virtue with wisdom rather than effort with knowledge.

kurals.tamil:
குடிசெய்வல் என்னும் ஒருவற்குத் தெய்வம்
மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந் துறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudiseyval ennum oruvarkuth theyvam
madidhatruth thaanmun thurum.
kurals.meaning: When a person resolves ‘I will raise my family’, fortune itself tucks up its garment and hurries ahead to help.
kurals.elementary: Have you noticed that when you really decide to clean your room, things suddenly seem to fall into place? Valluvar says that when someone truly decides to lift up their family, it is as if heaven rolls up its sleeves and runs ahead to help.
kurals.university: The striking image is madi tharru (மடிதற்று, ‘having tucked up the fold of its garment’), the gesture of someone girding up to work or run, so that theyvam (தெய்வம்) mun urum (முந்துறும், ‘comes forward first’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses theyvam as oozh (ஊழ், ‘destiny, fate’), keeping with the Kural's chapter 38; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a deity tightening its garment; Karunanidhi, rationalising, calls it the force of nature known as divine action. Pope gives ‘With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.’ The verb kudiseyval (‘I will make my family’) is a first-person vow, continuing 1021. The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demigods, being pleased by sacrifices, will also please you, and thus, by cooperation between men and demigods, prosperity will reign for all.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes a partnership in which human effort offered rightly draws divine help, and prosperity follows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the divine meets the person who first commits to the work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.11 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good thematic fit on divine help answering human effort, though the Gita's mechanism is sacrifice.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Psalmist says that unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labour in vain.
christianity.explanation: The psalm teaches that human building succeeds only when God takes part in it.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense that unseen help joins the family-builder, but it puts God first where the Kural puts the human vow first.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; related theme with a reversed emphasis.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties God's change of a people's condition to the change they first make in themselves.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, divine help follows a human resolve.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; a strong match on divine response to human initiative.

judaism.quote_or_event: “do His will as though it were your will, so that He will do your will as though it were His.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel teaches that a person who makes God's purposes his own will find God taking up his purposes in turn.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly promises that heaven runs ahead to help the one who commits to a worthy task.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good reciprocal structure, though the commitment is to God's will rather than to one's family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “You yourselves must strive; the Buddhas only point the way.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says no outside power does the work for you; teachers only show the road.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that everything starts with personal resolve, but unlike the Kural it promises no deity running ahead to help.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 276 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it matches the stress on personal resolve but rejects the divine-help half of the couplet.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi tells King Srenika that a person's own conduct, not any outside protector, makes happiness or misery.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, which has no creator God, reads the Kural's ‘theyvam’ as the fruit of one's own action, much as Varadarasanar glosses it as destiny.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the stress on one's own agency but denies the outside divine help the couplet pictures, so it is a next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop's fable of Hercules and the Waggoner, a carter whose wagon is stuck prays to Hercules without lifting a finger; the god tells him to put his shoulder to the wheel and whip his horses, and only then to call on him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The god helps the one who is already working, not the one who waits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural exactly: divine help comes running to the person who has started the work.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase of a well-known fable; a near one-to-one match on the gods helping those who help themselves.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Terence's proverb that fortune helps the brave (fortes fortuna adiuvat), later repeated by Cicero and Seneca, holds that luck favours those who act boldly.
philosophy.explanation: Roman moralists turned the line into a maxim that bold, committed action draws good fortune to it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fortune that hurries ahead of the committed family-builder is the same idea.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous proverb, not checked verbatim this session; Terence was a dramatist, so this is a popular rather than strictly philosophical source.

kurals.tamil:
சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும் தம்குடியைத்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Soozhaamal thaane mudiveydhum thamkudiyaith
thaazhaadhu unjatru bavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who strive without delay to raise their family, the work reaches its goal by itself, even before they have planned it out.
kurals.elementary: When you practise piano every day without putting it off, one day a hard song just seems to play itself. Valluvar says that when people keep working for their family without delay, success often arrives before they even sit down to plan it.
kurals.university: Soozhaamal (சூழாமல், ‘without deliberating, without planning’) and thaane (தானே, ‘of itself’) frame the promise that the task mudiveydhum (முடிவெய்தும், ‘reaches completion’) for those who thaazhaadhu unjatrupavar (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், ‘strive without delay’). Kesikan, following the older commentary, attributes this to divine aid (தெய்வ உதவியால்), linking it to 1023; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it naturalistically, saying the capacity to finish comes to the prompt worker unsought. Karunanidhi has victories ‘pile up of themselves.’ Pope translates ‘Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that steady action as duty, without fretting over results, itself brings the highest attainment.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the outcome comes of itself to the one who simply keeps working.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it shares the idea that results follow steady work, but its goal is spiritual.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that the slack hand brings poverty but the hand of the diligent makes rich.
christianity.explanation: The sage links prosperity directly to diligent work.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say success comes almost naturally to the person who works without slackening.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; a solid thematic match.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says a person receives the good that matches his own striving.
islam.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that the result follows from the effort itself.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it links reward to effort, though not the speed of the Kural's result.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the laborers are indolent, and the reward is great, and the master of the house is insistent.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon warns that the time is short and the work great, so delay is costly and the reward large.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges striving without delay and promises that great reward follows.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:15 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it matches the urgency, not the promise of effortless success.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill's rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala that steady, honest work makes wealth grow on its own, like an anthill.
buddhism.tie_back: Its image of riches mounting up by themselves matches the Kural's success that ‘comes of itself’ to the steady worker.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (verse line breaks joined); a good fit on effortless-seeming growth from steady effort in household life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it?”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that knowing and discussing the path achieves nothing without actually walking it.
jainism.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that doing, not deliberating, brings results, though for liberation rather than family welfare.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the stress on action over deliberation, but the context is monastic practice, so it is a next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Through work men grow rich in flocks and substance, and working they are much better loved by the immortals”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod promises his brother that steady farm work brings both wealth and the favour of the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says prosperity flows naturally to the one who keeps working.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 293-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (the translator's note marker is omitted); a good fit for a household farmer's success.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so that repeated practice makes good action second nature.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, steady practice turns hard actions into habits that then come almost without effort.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the Kural's claim that for the constant striver the work completes itself without deliberation.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; an explanatory parallel on habit rather than a direct statement about effortless success.

kurals.tamil:
குற்றம் இலனாய்க் குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச்
சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kutram ilanaaik kudiseydhu vaazhvaanaich
sutramaach chutrum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world gathers around the person who raises his family without doing wrong, and treats him as its own kin.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kind neighbour who works hard for her family and never cheats anyone. Soon the whole street treats her like family, bringing food and asking her advice. Valluvar says that is what happens to honest family-builders: everyone wants to be their relative.
kurals.university: Kutram ilanaai (குற்றம் இலனாய், ‘being without fault’) is the condition: the family must be raised by blameless means. The reward is a pun on sutram (சுற்றம், ‘kin, relatives’) and sutrum (சுற்றும், ‘surrounds, encircles’): the ulagu (உலகு, ‘world’) surrounds him as if it were his own relatives. Varadarasanar and Kesikan say people seek to become his kin; Pappaiah narrows ulagu to ‘the great’ (உயர்ந்தோர்), in keeping with the commentarial habit of reading ulagam as the worthy. Pope translates ‘The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that the world gathers behind and imitates the person of exemplary conduct.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's blameless family-builder whom the world surrounds, the exemplary person draws everyone to follow.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it shares the image of the world drawn to the exemplary person, though it speaks of imitation rather than kinship.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs tells the reader to keep mercy and truth close, and so to find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
christianity.explanation: The sage promises that a life of faithfulness wins goodwill from people as well as from God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says a blameless life makes the world want to be one's kin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; a reasonable match on favour won by integrity.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises that God will place love for the righteous in people's hearts.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the upright are surrounded by affection as if they were family.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; a strong match on righteous living winning people's affection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “which is the straight path that a man should choose for himself? One which is an honor to the person adopting it, and [on account of which] honor [accrues] to him from others.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince defines the right path as one that is honourable in itself and earns honour from others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's blameless family-builder, embraced by the world, follows exactly this path.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:1 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (bracketed words are the translator's); a good fit on integrity winning esteem.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is full of faith and virtue, and possesses good repute and wealth — he is respected everywhere, in whatever land he travels.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the virtuous householder of good name and honest wealth is honoured wherever he goes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the world embraces the blameless one who has raised his family.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 303 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match that even pairs virtue with wealth, as the Kural pairs blamelessness with raising the family.

jainism.quote_or_event: Hemachandra's Yogashastra lists, as the first quality of a householder fit for the Jain path, wealth acquired by just and honest means (nyaya-sampanna-vibhava).
jainism.explanation: Jain lay ethics makes honest earning the foundation of a good household life.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘without fault’ condition for raising one's family.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Yogashastra, Book 1 (the marganusari qualities of the householder)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested doctrine, not checked against a live translation this session; it matches the blameless-means condition but not the world's embrace.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch tells how Theseus gathered the scattered villages of Attica into one city, Athens, and the people came together under him as one community.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's work for his people turned many separate households into a single family-like city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It loosely matches the Kural's picture of people drawn around a builder as his own kin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a loose match, since Theseus unifies a city by policy and not because of his blamelessness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For nothing inspires love, nothing conciliates affection, like virtue. Why, in a certain sense we may be said to feel affection even for men we have never seen, owing to their honesty and virtue.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that friendship springs from the natural pull of virtue: goodness draws affection so strongly that we love even good men we have never met.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's promise that people gather around the blameless man and treat him as their own kin.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia, ch. 8 (§§27-28) (tr. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (Shuckburgh, eBook #2808, chapter 8). Strong-to-partial match: virtue wins the affection of others, but Cicero does not speak of a householder who raises his family without wrong.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லாண்மை என்பது ஒருவற்குத் தான்பிறந்த
இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallaanmai enbadhu oruvarkuth thaanpirandha
illaanmai aakkik kolal.
kurals.meaning: True manliness means making oneself the one who leads and looks after the household one was born into.
kurals.elementary: Some people think being strong means winning fights. Valluvar says real strength is when you grow up and become the person your family can lean on, the one who takes care of things at home.
kurals.university: The couplet redefines nallaanmai (நல்லாண்மை, ‘good manliness, true valour’) by rhyming it with illaanmai (இல்லாண்மை, ‘mastery of the household’): real valour is aakkik kolal (ஆக்கிக் கொளல், ‘making one's own’) the governance of the home one was born in (thaan pirandha, தான் பிறந்த). Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as taking on the ruling of one's birth-family; Pappaiah again extends it to house and country; Karunanidhi reverses the emphasis, saying the able ruler brings glory to the family of his birth. Pope gives ‘To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is far better to discharge one’s prescribed duties, even though faultily, than another’s duties perfectly.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that a person's own duty, the one that falls to him by his station, is the one he must take up.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly asks a person to take up the duty of the house he was born into.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; svadharma parallels the duty of one's birth-house, though the Gita speaks of caste duty rather than family leadership.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes providing for one's own household a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats taking charge of one's own family as the measure of a person.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a close match on responsibility for one's own house.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them and a man is the guardian of his family and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every person is a shepherd responsible for those in his care, and a man for his family.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of ruling and caring for one's household is the same guardianship.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a near one-to-one match on household guardianship.

judaism.quote_or_event: After their father's death, Joseph reassures his frightened brothers that he will sustain them and their little ones, and he comforts them.
judaism.explanation: Joseph, now powerful, uses his position to provide for the whole family he was born into.
judaism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's ideal of making oneself the head and support of one's birth-family.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Hebrew text checked on Sefaria; a strong narrative illustration.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having supported me I shall support them, I shall do their duties, I shall keep the family tradition, I shall make myself worthy of my inheritance”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the duties a grown child takes on toward parents and the family line.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal of taking charge of the household one was born into.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (list numbering removed); a close match on duty to one's birth-family.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Kalpa Sutra tells that Mahavira, out of regard for his parents, resolved not to renounce the world while they lived, and became a monk only after their death.
jainism.explanation: Even the future Tirthankara honoured his duty to the family he was born into before leaving it.
jainism.tie_back: It shows Jainism recognising the claim of one's birth-family that the Kural celebrates, though only as a stage before renunciation.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against Jacobi's wording this session; the fit is partial because Mahavira ultimately leaves the household.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus returns to Ithaca after twenty years, drives out the suitors who are wasting his estate, and takes his place again as head of his father's house.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's last and greatest labour is restoring order in his own household.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that true valour is mastery of one's own home.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a good fit, though the story turns on violent revenge rather than steady care.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thus it is clear that household management attends more to men than to the acquisition of inanimate things, and to human excellence more than to the excellence of property which we call wealth, and to the virtue of freemen more than to the virtue of slaves.”
philosophy.explanation: After describing the head of the household as ruling his children like a king, by love and seniority (I.12), Aristotle concludes that running a household is chiefly about the excellence of its people, not about wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle treats leading and caring for one's household as a test of a man's character.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Politics Book I, Part XIII). Next-best match: Aristotle analyses household rule rather than calling it the proof of manliness, and his account rests on hierarchies (over women and slaves) that the Kural does not share.

kurals.tamil:
அமரகத்து வன்கண்ணர் போலத் தமரகத்தும்
ஆற்றுவார் மேற்றே பொறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Amaragaththu vankannar polath thamaragaththum
aatruvaar metre porai.
kurals.meaning: Just as on the battlefield the burden falls on the fearless, so within a family the burden rests on those able to bear it.
kurals.elementary: In a soccer game, the toughest players stand in front when the other team attacks. Valluvar says families are the same: when trouble comes, the strongest, most capable person has to step forward and carry the load.
kurals.university: The couplet balances amaragaththu (அமரகத்து, ‘in the battlefield’) against thamaragaththum (தமரகத்தும், ‘among one's own people too’); the vankannar (வன்கண்ணர், ‘the hard-eyed, the fearless’) of war correspond to the aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், ‘those who are able’) in the family, and on them falls porai (பொறை, ‘burden, load’). Varadarasanar stresses that though many are born into a family, the burden lies on the capable. Text note: ytamizh.com reads தமரகத்தும் (with the inclusive -um) while thirukkural.net prints தமரகத்து ஆற்றுவார்; the meaning is the same and this edition follows the -um reading, which Pope's ‘Amid his kindred so’ also reflects.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Considering your specific duty as a kṣatriya, you should know that there is no better engagement for you than fighting on religious principles; and so there is no need for hesitation.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the warrior's duty is to stand and fight, not to shrink back.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses exactly this warrior who does not shrink as its model for the family member who carries the load.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it matches the battlefield half of the simile, not the family half.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says those with strength must carry the burdens of the weaker members of the community.
christianity.tie_back: It is almost the Kural's rule: the burden belongs to those able to bear it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a near one-to-one match on the strong bearing the load.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart”
islam.explanation: The Prophet prizes strength in the believer and tells him not to lose heart.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours the strong who stand firm, though it does not speak of carrying the family.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it praises strength and steadfastness, which only partly matches the burden-bearing theme.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that when no one else steps up, you must be the one who takes responsibility.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the load falls on whoever has the strength to take it.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:5 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on stepping forward to carry responsibility.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patient endurance to a war elephant that stands firm under a hail of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: Its battlefield image of steady endurance matches the Kural's fearless warrior who bears the brunt.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 320 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the image matches closely, but the burden borne is abuse, not a family's welfare.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns his disciple not to stumble like a weak porter who leaves the smooth road under his load.
jainism.tie_back: The image of the strong and weak burden-bearer echoes the Kural's point that the load needs someone able to carry it, though the Jain load is the monastic path.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only the burden-bearer image is shared, so this is a next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the Trojans break through to the Greek ships, Ajax son of Telamon stands almost alone on the decks, fending off fire and spears to protect the whole army.
greek_mythology.explanation: With the other leaders wounded, the burden of defence falls on the one hero strong enough to bear it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's battlefield image in action: the load rests on the one who can carry it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a strong match for the warrior half of the simile.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Because in the army the most hazardous services are assigned to the bravest soldiers: a general sends his choicest troops to attack the enemy in a midnight ambuscade, to reconnoitre his line of march, or to drive the hostile garrisons from their strong places.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca explains why God sends hardship to the best of men: as a general gives the hardest tasks to his finest troops, they say not 'he has dealt hardly with me' but 'he has judged well of me'.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca uses the Kural's own battlefield image: the heaviest load falls on those strong enough to bear it.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Of Providence (De Providentia) 4.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Providence). The Wikisource text has no section numbers, so 4.8 follows the standard Latin numbering. Strong match on the battlefield image of burdens falling on the brave; Seneca applies it to divine providence, not to family duty.

kurals.tamil:
குடிசெய்வார்க் கில்லை பருவம் மடிசெய்து
மானங் கருதக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudiseyvaark killai paruvam madiseydhu
maanang karudhak kedum.
kurals.meaning: Those who raise a family have no ‘right season’ to wait for; if they idle or stand on their dignity, the family is ruined.
kurals.elementary: If you wait for the ‘perfect day’ to do your chores, it never comes, and the mess just grows. Valluvar says people who care for a family can't wait for a perfect time or think a job is beneath them; they just have to get going.
kurals.university: Paruvam (பருவம், ‘season, proper time’) is denied to the kudiseyvaar (குடிசெய்வார், ‘those who make the family’): any time is the time. The second line names two enemies, madi (மடி, ‘sloth’, the theme of chapter 61) and maanam karudhal (மானம் கருதல், ‘considering one's pride or honour’), either of which makes the family kedum (கெடும், ‘perish’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read maanam as standing on one's dignity, refusing humble work; Karunanidhi reads it as being shaken by insults directed at oneself. Pope gives ‘Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear; / ’Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says work is always better than inaction and that even bodily survival needs it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects idleness, since nothing can be kept going without work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a good match on rejecting sloth, though it does not address waiting for the right season.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher warns that the farmer who keeps waiting for perfect weather never plants or harvests.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘there is no season’: waiting for the ideal time means ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com; a near one-to-one match on not waiting for the right season.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that people waste their health and spare time, thinking there will always be more.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns against letting time slip by in idleness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a partial match on wasting time, without the family context or the warning about pride.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off important work until a convenient time that may never come.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's point that the family-builder has no ‘proper season’ to wait for.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match on not waiting for the right time, applied to study rather than family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who says it is too hot, too cold, too late, and leaves things undone, the opportunities for good go past such men. But he who does not regard cold or heat any more than a blade of grass and who does his duties manfully, does not fall away from happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns the householder that making excuses about weather and time loses every chance of prosperity.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost the Kural itself: the one who raises a family has no season to wait for.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match, addressed to a householder.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that life falls like a dead leaf, so he must never be careless for a moment.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain call to constant heedfulness (apramada) matches the Kural's rejection of waiting and idling, though it aims at liberation rather than household welfare.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's parenthesis kept); a strong match on never delaying, with a different goal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work: industry makes work go well”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that the farmer who delays his work ends with an empty barn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a household is ruined by sloth and by waiting for a later time.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days, passage at ll. 405-413 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one match on delay ruining a household.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius by urging him to seize each hour, because while we put things off, life runs past us.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that postponement wastes the one thing we truly own, our time.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's warning that waiting for a right season ruins the work.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the wording was not checked against a live translation this session, though the letter's theme is well known.

kurals.tamil:
இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ குடும்பத்தைக்
குற்ற மறைப்பான் உடம்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Idumbaikke kolkalam kollo kudumbaththaik
kutra maraippaan udambu.
kurals.meaning: Is the body of one who shields his family from harm only a vessel for suffering?
kurals.elementary: Think of a parent who works late, carries heavy bags, and gets up at night when the baby cries. Their body is tired and sore. Valluvar asks: is that body only made for hardship? His answer is that their toil is also full of love and worth.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is the udambu (உடம்பு, ‘body’) of the one who kutram maraippaan (குற்றம் மறைப்பான், ‘wards off harm’ from his kudumbam, குடும்பம், ‘family’) merely an idumbaikke kolkalam (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம், ‘a vessel for suffering alone’)? The particle kollo (கொல்லோ) marks wonder or doubt. Varadarasanar reads it plainly as ‘is his body only a home for suffering?’, conceding the hardship; Kesikan and Pappaiah draw the implied answer, that it is also a vessel of joy; Karunanidhi says such a person is honoured as one born to bear suffering. Pope gives ‘Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, / Who would his household screen from every ill?’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that bodily pain and pleasure come and go like seasons and must be borne with steadiness.
hinduism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's picture of a body that must bear hardship for the sake of duty.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it matches endurance of bodily hardship, without the family context.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus teaches that no one has greater love than the person who lays down his life for his friends.
christianity.explanation: Self-sacrifice for others is presented as the highest form of love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's body given over to hardship to protect the family is this kind of love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; a thematic match on sacrifice for others.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands believers to shield their families from ruin.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's family-protector, the believer is charged with guarding his household from harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it matches the duty to shield one's family, though the harm meant is spiritual.

judaism.quote_or_event: Nehemiah, rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under threat, tells the people not to fear but to remember the great and awesome Lord and fight for their brothers, sons, daughters, wives and homes.
judaism.explanation: The builders work with one hand and keep a weapon in the other, to protect their families while they build.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural's picture of a body spent in shielding one's family.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 4:8 (Hebrew numbering; 4:14 in English Bibles), Tanakh via Sefaria
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Hebrew text checked on Sefaria; a strong match on toiling to protect one's family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahakapi Jataka the Bodhisatta, born as a monkey king, stretches his own body as a bridge across a river so his troop can escape the king's archers, and is fatally hurt doing so.
buddhism.explanation: The monkey king turns his own body into the means of his people's safety.
buddhism.tie_back: It vividly answers the Kural's question about the body of the one who shields his family.
buddhism.source: Mahakapi Jataka (Jataka No. 407, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase of a well-known Jataka, not checked against the Cowell text this session; a strong match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that no family member can share the suffering that one's own karma brings.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism sees bodily suffering as one's own karma and the family as no refuge, so it offers a contrast to the Kural's ideal of suffering for one's family.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; included as an honest contrast, since Jain doctrine counsels detachment from family rather than toil for it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus, chained to a rock as punishment for giving fire and the arts to humankind, endures endless bodily torment rather than betray those he protected.
greek_mythology.explanation: His body becomes a vessel of suffering because he chose to shield and raise up humanity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's question about the body of the one who protects his own.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a good fit on suffering for those one protects, though humanity is not literally his family.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is true of the good man too that he does many acts for the sake of his friends and his country, and if necessary dies for them; for he will throw away both wealth and honours and in general the goods that are objects of competition, gaining for himself nobility …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that the good man's sacrifices for others, even his life, are not losses, because he wins for himself the greater good of nobility.
philosophy.tie_back: This gives the answer the Kural's question implies: the protector's suffering body is not a mere vessel of pain, since his sacrifice is what makes him noble.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book IX ch. 8). Partial match: self-sacrifice for others as nobility; Aristotle speaks of friends and country rather than family, and of losing goods rather than bodily suffering.

kurals.tamil:
இடுக்கண்கால் கொன்றிட வீழும் அடுத்தூன்றும்
நல்லாள் இலாத குடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Idukkankaal kondrida veezhum aduththoondrum
nallaal ilaadha kudi.
kurals.meaning: A family with no good person to stand by and prop it up will fall like a tree when misfortune strikes at its root.
kurals.elementary: A young tree needs a stick tied beside it so the wind doesn't knock it over. Valluvar says a family is like that tree: when hard times blow, it needs a strong, caring person standing beside it, or it will fall.
kurals.university: The image is of a tree: idukkan (இடுக்கண், ‘misfortune’) strikes at its kaal (கால், ‘foot, base’) and kondrida (கொன்றிட, ‘cutting, killing’) brings it down, unless there is a nallaal (நல்லாள், ‘good person’) who aduththu oondrum (அடுத்து ஊன்றும், ‘stands close and props it up’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah make the axe explicit (துன்பமாகிய கோடாரி, ‘the axe of misfortune’), and Kesikan names the tree; Pappaiah reads nallaal as ‘good children’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning 1021's vow into a warning about its absence. Pope gives ‘When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall, / If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.’ The text is identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “With the destruction of the dynasty, the eternal family tradition is vanquished, and thus the rest of the family becomes involved in irreligion.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna fears that once a family's leading men fall, the whole family collapses.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning: a family without its supporters falls.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.39 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a strong fit on family collapse, though spoken by Arjuna in a doubt that Krishna goes on to answer.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus says that a house built on sand falls when the rains, floods and winds beat on it, and great is its fall.
christianity.explanation: A house without a solid foundation cannot survive the storm.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows a household with nothing to hold it up collapsing under misfortune.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; the image matches but the parable is about obeying Jesus's words.

islam.quote_or_event: “A faithful believer to a faithful believer is like the bricks of a wall, enforcing each other.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet, lacing his fingers together, describes believers as bricks that hold each other up.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a community stands only when its members prop one another up.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a good fit on mutual support holding a structure up.

judaism.quote_or_event: Kohelet observes that two are better than one, for if one falls the other lifts him up, but woe to the one who falls alone with no one to raise him.
judaism.explanation: The sage warns that someone with no companion to help has nothing to save him when he falls.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's family with no one to prop it up suffers this same fall.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked verbatim this session; a strong match on having no one to hold you up.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges building, through effort, a refuge that disaster cannot sweep away.
buddhism.tie_back: It answers the Kural's warning from the other side: steady effort makes a refuge that misfortune cannot overturn.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 25 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a partial match, since the island is inner liberation rather than family support.

jainism.quote_or_event: “My father would have spent all he possessed, for my sake; but he could not rid me of my pains, hence I say that I am without protection.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Anathi explains that even a devoted family could not protect him from suffering, which led him to renounce the world.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism treats the family's support as finally unable to hold up the soul, so it gives an honest contrast to the Kural's faith in the family's prop.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the theme of who can prop up a person in distress but draws the opposite conclusion, so it is a contrastive next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Achilles kills Hector, Troy's great defender, the city's lament is as though all Ilion were already burning, and with its prop gone Troy soon falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector was the one man holding up his city and family; his death leaves them defenceless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Kural's image exactly: a house with no one to prop it falls when misfortune strikes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; a strong match on a family and city collapsing once its support is gone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Or how can prosperity be guarded and preserved without friends? The greater it is, the more exposed is it to risk. And in poverty and in other misfortunes men think friends are the only refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Opening his account of friendship, Aristotle says that without others to stand by it no fortune can be kept safe, and that in misfortune they are the only support.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's family with no one to prop it up, Aristotle's prosperity left without friends is exposed to fall when misfortune strikes.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book VIII ch. 1). Next-best match: the idea of needing a supporter in misfortune is shared, but Aristotle speaks of friends and an individual's prosperity, not of a good man holding up a family, and he has no tree image.
